title: Fewest Checkpoints for Every Trip
statement:
Cars drive along one straight road. trips[i] = [start, end] says that car i drives over every position from start to end, both ends included.

You may place checkpoints at any positions. A checkpoint at x sees every car whose trip covers x. Return the smallest number of checkpoints needed so that every car is seen at least once.

examples.why: A checkpoint at 4 sees the first two cars, one at 9 sees the third, and one anywhere from 10 to 12 sees the last.
Ends are included, so a checkpoint at 3 sees the first two cars. The third needs its own, for example at 5.
Putting the first checkpoint at the end of the earliest-starting trip (10) wastes it. Positions 3 and 5 cover all three.

hints: Look at the trip that ends first. Some checkpoint must see it, so one must sit somewhere inside it. Where inside it is the most useful spot?
Pushing that checkpoint as far right as possible, to the trip's end, can only see more trips, never fewer.
Sort by end. Place a checkpoint at the first end, skip every trip that starts at or before it, and repeat with the next unseen trip.

explain.intuition:
Take the trip that finishes earliest. It needs a checkpoint somewhere in its range. Every other trip ends at or after it, so any trip that covers some point of this range and is still going also covers its end point. Placing the checkpoint at that end point therefore sees at least as many cars as any other choice. That is the greedy step, and it is safe.

After placing it, every trip that starts at or before the checkpoint is seen. The next unseen trip in end order becomes the new "earliest finisher", and you repeat. It is the classic interval-scheduling argument: the count of checkpoints equals the largest number of trips that pairwise do not overlap.
steps: Place the first checkpoint at the end of the first trip; set count = 1.
For each later trip, if its start is ≤ the last checkpoint, it is already seen.
Otherwise place a new checkpoint at its end and increment count.
pitfalls: Using < instead of ≤ when testing the start. Ends are included, so a trip starting exactly at the checkpoint is seen.
Sorting by start and placing checkpoints at the first trip's end. A long early trip like [1, 10] then hides shorter ones inside it.
In languages with 32-bit ints, writing the comparator as a[1] − b[1] overflows at the extreme values.

solutions.title: Sort by start, shrink the shared window
solutions.idea: Walk trips by start, keeping the smallest end of the current group. A trip that starts after that end must open a new group.

solutions.title: Sort by end, greedy checkpoints
solutions.idea: Always place the next checkpoint at the end of the earliest-finishing unseen trip.

followups: Return the checkpoint positions too, not just how many.
Each checkpoint can see at most k cars. Does the greedy still work?
